description: How an operating system virtualises the processor and memory, lets programs share safely, stores data persistently and talks to devices, learned by reading, modifying and measuring a real teaching kernel. Taught to the depth of a leading operating systems course.
modelledOn: Arpaci-Dusseau, Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces
Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts
Tanenbaum and Bos, Modern Operating Systems
The xv6 teaching operating system and its commentary
outcomes: Explain the structure of an operating system, system calls, kernel and user modes, and the boot process.
Describe process and thread life cycles and implement and evaluate CPU scheduling algorithms.
Write correct concurrent programs with locks, semaphores, condition variables and monitors, and detect and prevent deadlock.
Analyse memory management with paging, segmentation, virtual memory and page replacement.
Explain file system design, disk scheduling, I/O subsystems and device drivers.
Describe virtual machines, multiprocessor operating systems and the design of mobile operating systems.

units.title: Introduction to operating systems
topics: What an OS does: abstraction, virtualisation, resource management, protection; history from batch to cloud and mobile
Kernel and user mode, system calls, traps and interrupts; the boot sequence
OS structures: monolithic, layered, microkernel, modules, exokernel; Linux, Windows and xv6 compared
Shell, processes and system programming in C: fork, exec, wait, pipes, signals
Building and running xv6 in an emulator; reading kernel code

units.title: Process management
topics: Processes: states, PCB, context switch, creation and termination; the process tree
Threads: user and kernel threads, pthreads, thread pools; why threads
CPU scheduling: FCFS, SJF, SRTF, priority, round robin, multilevel feedback queues; metrics and Gantt charts
Real-time scheduling (RM, EDF), proportional share and the Linux CFS
Implementing a scheduler in xv6 and measuring turnaround and response time

units.title: Concurrency and synchronisation
topics: Race conditions, critical sections, atomicity; Peterson's algorithm and hardware primitives (test-and-set, compare-and-swap)
Locks, spinlocks, semaphores, condition variables, monitors; producer-consumer, readers-writers, dining philosophers
Deadlock: conditions, resource allocation graphs, prevention, avoidance (banker's algorithm), detection and recovery
Concurrency bugs: atomicity and order violations; lock-free structures in brief
Inter-process communication: shared memory, message passing, pipes, sockets

units.title: Memory management
topics: Address spaces, address binding, logical versus physical addresses; base and bounds
Contiguous allocation and fragmentation; segmentation; free-space management (first fit, best fit, buddy, slab)
Paging: page tables, TLBs, multi-level and inverted page tables; address translation worked examples
Virtual memory: demand paging, page faults, copy-on-write; replacement (FIFO, LRU, clock, optimal); thrashing and the working set
Memory in xv6: page tables, allocation, implementing lazy allocation

units.title: File systems
topics: Files, directories, links, permissions; the file system interface and the VFS layer
Storage layout: inodes, extents, bitmaps, directories; FAT, ext4, NTFS compared
Crash consistency: fsck, journaling, copy-on-write (ZFS, Btrfs), log-structured file systems
Caching, buffering, read-ahead; disk scheduling (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN); SSDs and flash translation layers
RAID and reliability; network file systems

units.title: I/O system
topics: I/O hardware: controllers, ports, buses, polling, interrupts, DMA
The I/O subsystem: device drivers, character and block devices, buffering, spooling
Writing a simple device driver; interrupt handling in the kernel
Clocks, timers and power management

units.title: Protection, security and virtual machines
topics: Protection domains, access control lists, capabilities; user authentication and privilege
OS security: buffer overflows, privilege escalation, sandboxing, address-space randomisation
Virtual machines: hypervisors (type 1 and 2), trap-and-emulate, paravirtualisation, hardware support, nested page tables
Containers: namespaces, cgroups, images; VMs versus containers

units.title: Multiple processor systems and mobile operating systems
topics: Multiprocessor scheduling, load balancing, processor affinity, cache coherence effects, NUMA
Distributed and cluster operating systems in brief
Mobile operating systems: Android architecture (Linux kernel, ART, Binder, app sandbox), iOS; power management, app life cycle, permissions
Case study: the Linux kernel and how to contribute; the future of operating systems

schedule.title: What an OS does and its structures
schedule.exercise: Compare monolithic, microkernel and layered OS designs in a short table of trade-offs, and say which best fits a small embedded device.

tasks.title: Trace a system call from user mode to kernel mode in a step visualiser, labelling the trap, the mode switch and the return
List five resources an OS virtualises for a process (CPU, memory, files) and explain what would break if one were not virtualised
Compare how xv6, Linux and Windows structure their kernels, and justify which structure a student OS project should copy and why

schedule.title: Shell, system programming and xv6
schedule.exercise: Write a short program design (on paper) for a shell that forks a child, execs a command and waits for it, noting where errors can occur.

tasks.title: Write a C program that forks a child process, has it exec a command, and the parent waits for and reports the exit status
Build a two-process pipeline with a pipe so one process's output becomes another's input, matching the behaviour of a shell pipe
Build and boot xv6 in the emulator, step through the first few lines of kernel code executed after boot, and identify where the first process starts

schedule.title: Processes, threads and scheduling
schedule.exercise: Draw a Gantt chart by hand for FCFS, SJF and round robin scheduling of five given processes, and compute the average waiting time for each.

tasks.title: Step through a process's states from creation to termination in the visualiser and identify the event that causes each transition
Compare FCFS, SJF and round robin scheduling on the same five processes and determine which gives the lowest average waiting time
Create three pthreads that increment a shared counter without synchronisation, show the final count is wrong, then fix it with a lock

schedule.title: Advanced scheduling and xv6
schedule.exercise: Explain, with a worked example, why a multilevel feedback queue can starve a long process, and propose a fix.

tasks.title: Simulate rate-monotonic and earliest-deadline-first scheduling for three periodic tasks and determine which one meets all deadlines
Implement a round robin scheduler in xv6 and measure the turnaround and response time for a set of test processes
Compare the Linux CFS virtual runtime mechanism with multilevel feedback queues on a scenario with one interactive and one batch process

schedule.title: Synchronisation
schedule.exercise: Work through the dining philosophers problem on paper, show where a naive solution deadlocks, and describe the fix.

tasks.title: Implement a producer-consumer solution with a semaphore and a shared buffer, and show it does not lose or duplicate items under load
Trace a race condition on a shared counter step by step in the visualiser, showing the exact interleaving that produces a wrong result
Apply the banker's algorithm to decide whether a requested resource allocation is safe, and show the unsafe state it would have avoided

schedule.title: Concurrency bugs and IPC
schedule.exercise: Compare shared memory and message passing for two cooperating processes, and state which is easier to reason about and why.

tasks.title: Build two processes that communicate over a named pipe and a socket, and compare the setup each required
Find and fix an atomicity violation in a given multi-threaded program that updates two related variables without a single lock
Find and fix an ordering violation where one thread reads a flag before another thread that should set it first has run, visible as an intermittent failure

schedule.title: Memory management
schedule.exercise: Work a paging address-translation example by hand for a given page size and page table, converting three logical addresses to physical ones.

tasks.title: Step through address translation for a given logical address using a two-level page table and identify the frame it maps to
Compare first-fit and best-fit allocation on the same sequence of memory requests and show which leaves less fragmentation
Simulate a TLB with a given hit rate and compute the effective memory access time, then show the effect of doubling the hit rate

schedule.title: Virtual memory and xv6
schedule.exercise: Compare FIFO, LRU and optimal page replacement on the same reference string and compute the page faults each produces.

tasks.title: Run FIFO, LRU and optimal replacement on the same page reference string and compare the number of page faults for each
Simulate a demand-paging system under increasing load and identify the point where thrashing begins from the page fault rate
Implement lazy allocation for a memory region in xv6 so pages are only mapped on first access, and confirm it with a test program

schedule.title: File systems
schedule.exercise: Compare FAT, ext4 and NTFS on how each stores file metadata and handles large files, and recommend one for a low-power field device.

tasks.title: Create files and directories in a simulated Linux shell, inspect permissions and hard and soft links, and explain what each permission bit controls
Trace how an inode and its direct and indirect blocks locate the data of a file larger than the direct blocks can address
Simulate a crash during a file write with and without journaling enabled, and show journaling prevents the file system from being left inconsistent

schedule.title: Storage performance and reliability
schedule.exercise: Compute the seek pattern and total head movement for FCFS, SSTF and SCAN disk scheduling on the same sequence of requests.

tasks.title: Compare FCFS, SSTF and SCAN disk scheduling on the same request queue and compute the total head movement for each
Simulate an SSD's flash translation layer handling writes and show why random writes behave differently from a spinning disk
Compute the usable capacity and fault tolerance of RAID 0, 1 and 5 for the same four disks, and recommend one for a small file server

schedule.title: I/O systems
schedule.exercise: Compare polling, interrupt-driven and DMA-based I/O for transferring a large file, with a table of CPU involvement for each.

tasks.title: Trace an interrupt-driven I/O request from the device raising an interrupt to the driver completing the transfer
Write a simple character device driver in a simulated kernel and confirm a user program can read and write through it
Measure the CPU time saved by moving a large data transfer from polling to DMA in the simulated I/O subsystem

schedule.title: Protection, virtualisation and containers
schedule.exercise: Compare a type 1 hypervisor, a type 2 hypervisor and containers for isolating three untrusted applications, and recommend one with reasons.

tasks.title: Trigger a simulated buffer overflow in a vulnerable program and show how address-space randomisation and a stack canary would have stopped it
Compare trap-and-emulate virtualisation with paravirtualisation for a guest OS instruction, and explain why paravirtualisation needs a modified guest
Launch two containers sharing a kernel but isolated by namespaces and cgroups, and show one cannot see the other's processes or exceed its memory limit

schedule.title: Multiprocessor and mobile operating systems
schedule.exercise: Write a short comparison of Android's and iOS's app lifecycle and permission models, and explain one security trade-off each design makes.

tasks.title: Simulate scheduling five threads across two CPU cores with processor affinity and measure the effect of cache coherence traffic
Trace an Android app's lifecycle from launch through background to being killed for memory, and state what state is lost at each transition
Investigate a described Linux kernel contribution workflow and explain, step by step, how a patch moves from a mailing list to the mainline kernel
